newsitem.title: USA: U.S. export boom due to dollar/yen -- economist.
newsitem.headline: U.S. export boom due to dollar/yen -- economist.

text.p: Much of the recent steep growth in U.S. exports has been due to a favorable dollar/yen exchange rate, a leading economist said on Wednesday.
"A lot of the export boom has been a factor of (the exchange rate)," Michael Porter, Harvard Business School professor, told a group of lawmakers and their aides.
Porter, who is on the executive committee of the Council on Competitiveness, added that he believed Japanese companies are much more competitive than is widely thought.
The dollar fell to a record low of just below 80 yen in April 1995, although it has risen sharply since. At mid-day in New York on Wednesday, it was quoted at 115.80/85 yen.
Changes in exchange rates generally affect exports with a lag of one year or more, many economists believe.

"In our current fragile state in our economy where productivity growth is anemic and where investment is slow, I think we are more vulnerable today to the yen/dollar exchange rate," Porter said. "We should be concerned about that."
But the answer, the Harvard professor said, is not trying to manipulate the currency market. It is trying to tackle some of the fundamental economic problems facing the United States.
"If you have to have a low exchange rate to export, you're not competitive," Porter said.
If the dollar dropped back to 80 yen, the United States might be able to export more, but it would be poorer as a nation because it would have to pay more for its imports, Porter said.
He said that the United States has made progress over the last 10 years in improving its competitiveness as a nation, but that it still has a long way to go.

"We've made progress but we're far from there," he said, presenting previously-released Council on Competitiveness research showing just that. The Council consists of leaders from the business, labor and academic communities.
